items.prompt: This unit defines "evolutionary design" as:
choices: Shaping a system's structure incrementally, in response to requirements that actually arrive, so each new change stays roughly as cheap as the last
Designing every possible future requirement into the system on day one
Rewriting the whole system from scratch whenever a new requirement arrives
Choosing whichever design pattern is currently most popular
items.explanation: Evolutionary design reacts to real, arrived requirements rather than guessing at future ones, and reshapes the system just enough to keep the next change cheap — it's neither big-upfront-design (guessing everything now) nor rewrite-every-time (throwing away working code).
items.reference:
🌱 Evolutionary design — reshape incrementally, in response to real requirements
🚫 Not big-upfront-design (guess everything now)
🚫 Not rewrite-every-time (discard working code each round)
items.learnMore:
PostureAssumesBreaks because
Big upfront designYou can guess every future axis todayGuesses wrong half the time; unused flexibility still costs upkeep
Rewrite every changeEach requirement is cheap to re-deriveDiscards working, tested logic; gets slower as the system grows
Evolutionary designYou can react cheaply to real signalRequires correctly timing when a seam is earned

items.prompt: Which of these is the closest description of evolutionary design's core skill?
choices: Noticing when a second real variant justifies restructuring, rather than guessing upfront or rewriting on every change
Memorizing the Gang-of-Four pattern catalog
Always choosing the most flexible possible design for every function
Avoiding tests so the design stays easy to change
items.explanation: The skill evolutionary design depends on is timing — recognizing the point where a real second variant of something has shown up, which is the signal that a restructuring will actually pay off, rather than acting on a guess.
items.reference:
🌱 Evolutionary design — reshape incrementally, in response to real requirements
🚫 Not big-upfront-design (guess everything now)
🚫 Not rewrite-every-time (discard working code each round)

items.prompt: The open-closed principle says a module should be:
choices: Open for extension, closed for modification
Open for modification, closed for extension
Closed to all future changes once shipped
Open only to the original author
items.explanation: Open-closed means new behavior can be added (extension) without editing existing, already-tested code (modification stays closed) — e.g. appending a new PricingRule instead of editing calculateTotal's body.
items.reference:
🔓 Open for extension — new behavior can be added
🔒 Closed for modification — existing, tested code stays untouched
💰 A trade: one extra concept, in exchange for untouched existing tests
items.learnMore: In the Fernbridge pricing engine, before the fix every new discount/fee meant opening calculateTotal and editing its body — modification. After the fix, a new rule is a new object appended to the PricingRule list — extension. calculateTotal itself hasn't been edited since the seam was introduced. Open-closed isn't a rule to apply everywhere on principle — it's worth its cost exactly where a second real variant has shown up, not before.

items.prompt: In the pricing engine's round-2 fix, what makes calculateTotal "closed for modification"?
choices: It no longer needs to be edited when a new PricingRule is added — new rules are appended to a list instead
It has been marked as a read-only file so nobody can edit it
It has zero tests, so nothing depends on its exact behavior
It was deleted and replaced by a configuration file
items.explanation: calculateTotal reduces over whatever rules array is passed in and contains no rule-specific logic itself — adding a new rule means appending a new object to the array, never editing the function's body.
items.reference:

🔒 Closed for modification — existing, tested code stays untouched
💰 A trade: one extra concept, in exchange for untouched existing tests

items.prompt: In this unit's usage, a "seam" is:
choices: A point in the code where new behavior can be plugged in without editing what's already there
The visible line where two files were merged in git
A synonym for a bug in the design
A comment marking a section of code as deprecated
items.explanation: A seam is an explicit plug-in point — an interface, a registered list, an injected function — that lets new behavior be added without touching existing, already-tested code.
items.reference:
🔌 Seam — a plug-in point for new behavior, no edits to existing code
⏱️ Introduced just-in-time — when a second variant shows up
items.learnMore: The Fernbridge PricingRule interface plus its ordered array is a seam: volumeDiscountRule, couponRule, and later vipLoyaltyRule all plug into the same list without any of them needing to know about, or edit, the others. A seam doesn't have to be an interface — a registered list of callbacks, a strategy function passed as a parameter, or a plugin registry are all seams as long as they let new behavior attach without touching the existing, tested code around them.

items.prompt: Which of these is an example of a seam, as this unit uses the term?
choices: An ordered list of PricingRule objects that new rules get appended to
A single if-statement with no way to add more branches without editing it
A hardcoded 8% tax rate with no way to override it
A function with no parameters at all
items.explanation: An ordered, extensible list that new implementations can be appended to is a textbook seam — it's exactly what let Fernbridge add the VIP loyalty rule without touching any existing rule or its tests.
items.reference:
🔌 Seam — a plug-in point for new behavior, no edits to existing code
⏱️ Introduced just-in-time — when a second variant shows up

A seam doesn't have to be an interface — a registered list of callbacks, a strategy function passed as a parameter, or a plugin registry are all seams as long as they let new behavior attach without touching the existing, tested code around them.

items.prompt: A single if-statement with no interface, no list, and no way to add another case except editing its body is:
choices: Not a seam — any new case requires modifying the existing code directly
A seam, because if-statements can technically have else branches added
The same thing as open-closed
A speculative axis of change
items.explanation: A plain if-statement with no plug-in point is exactly what a seam is not — every new case means editing the existing code, which is modification, the thing open-closed and seams both exist to avoid once a second real variant shows up.

items.prompt: How does this unit resolve the tension between YAGNI ("don't build it until you need it") and "design for change"?
choices: By protecting the axis of change that has real, arrived signal now — not every hypothetical future axis
By always following YAGNI and never building any seams
By always designing for maximum flexibility on every axis, just in case
The two ideas are unrelated and never actually conflict
items.explanation: The resolution isn't picking one side permanently — it's recognizing which specific axis has real signal (a second variant has actually arrived) versus which is still speculation, and only building a seam for the former.
items.reference:
⚖️ YAGNI vs. design-for-change — not opposites, a targeting question
📶 Real signal now = second real variant arrived
🔮 Speculation = no evidence yet, just a guess
items.learnMore: At round 1, Fernbridge had exactly one discount rule — building a PricingRule abstraction then would have been speculation, so YAGNI correctly won. At round 2, a second, independent variant (the coupon) arrived and collided with the first, producing a real bug — that's signal, not speculation, so the seam earned its cost right there. The skill is telling those two moments apart, not picking a permanent side of the YAGNI-vs-design-for-change debate.

items.prompt: At round 1, Fernbridge had exactly one discount rule and no coupon requirement yet. Why was skipping the PricingRule abstraction the right call at that point?
choices: Because there was no second real variant yet — building the abstraction then would have been paying its cost for a benefit with no evidence behind it
Because abstractions are always wrong in every case
Because the team didn't know how to write interfaces yet
Because YAGNI says all future requirements should be ignored forever
items.explanation: With exactly one rule, there was nothing to be flexible about yet — the abstraction's cost (an interface, a list, extra indirection) would have been paid on a guess, not on evidence. The correct call was to wait for the second variant to show up.
items.reference:

📶 Real signal now = second real variant arrived
🔮 Speculation = no evidence yet, just a guess
items.learnMore: At round 1, Fernbridge had exactly one discount rule — building a PricingRule abstraction then would have been speculation, so YAGNI correctly won. At round 2, a second, independent variant (the coupon) arrived and collided with the first, producing a real bug — that's signal, not speculation, so the seam earned its cost right there. The skill is telling those two moments apart, not picking a permanent side of the YAGNI-vs-design-for-change debate.

items.prompt: "Just-in-time" seams means introducing a seam:
choices: When the second real variant of the same kind of thing arrives, not speculatively before it
As early as possible, always at the very start of a project
Only after the system has shipped and can never be changed again
Randomly, whenever the engineer feels like refactoring
items.explanation: Just-in-time means timed to real signal — the second concrete variant — rather than guessed at the first instance of something, when there's no evidence yet that a second one is coming.
items.reference:
1️⃣ One instance — no seam needed yet
2️⃣ Second instance — this is when the seam earns its cost
items.learnMore: Anything is "extensible" if you're willing to just edit it — one instance never needs a seam. A second instance is the point where a plain if-statement starts costing more to keep reading (and, as Fernbridge found out, more dangerous to get subtly wrong) than an interface would. Waiting for that second instance is what turns a seam's cost into something predictable rather than a bet on the future.

items.prompt: Why does this unit recommend waiting for a second real variant before introducing a seam, instead of building it at the very first instance?
choices: Because one instance provides no evidence about whether more variants are actually coming — building for it then is a guess, not a response to signal
Because seams are illegal to build until a system has shipped to production
Because the first instance of anything is always temporary code
Because YAGNI forbids ever building seams at all
items.explanation: One instance alone tells you nothing about whether a second is coming — introducing the seam there is a bet, not a response to real signal. A second instance is concrete evidence the axis is real, which is what makes the seam's cost worth paying.
items.reference:
1️⃣ One instance — no seam needed yet
2️⃣ Second instance — this is when the seam earns its cost

items.prompt: Across rounds 1 to 4, how does the cost of "fighting the design" (stacked if-statements) compare to "absorbing via a seam"?
choices: Fighting's cost grows faster each round, because every new if interacts with all the prior ones — the gap between the two widens over time
Both stay exactly equal forever, since they solve the same problem
Absorbing always costs more, in every single round, with no exceptions
Fighting is cheaper in every round because it requires writing less code
items.explanation: Fighting the design compounds because each new special case has to be reasoned about against every prior one sharing the same variable — the round-2 coupon bug is a direct example. Absorbing pays a one-time seam cost and then stays roughly flat per round, so the gap between the two widens with every additional round.
items.reference:
📈 Fighting: cost grows faster each round (interacts with every prior rule)
📉 Absorbing: one-time seam cost, then roughly flat per round
items.learnMore: In the unit's own numbers (2 hrs/round interaction penalty, seam introduced at round 2): fighting costs 2, 6, 12, 20 hours cumulative through rounds 1–4, while absorbing costs 2, 7, 9, 11 — identical at round 1, briefly costlier for absorbing at round 2 (the one-time seam setup), then cheaper and increasingly so from round 3 onward. Play with the interactive demo on this unit's L2 page to see the crossover move as you change the interaction penalty and which round the seam is introduced.

items.prompt: Why does "fighting the design" tend to produce bugs like the round-2 coupon/discount collision, rather than just costing more typing?
choices: Because stacked if-statements sharing one variable have no declared contract for what state that variable is in when each one runs, so later branches can guess wrong about it
Because if-statements are inherently slower to execute than function calls
Because JavaScript doesn't support if-statements properly
Because tests can't be written for if-statements
items.explanation: The bug wasn't a typo — it came from every branch reading and writing the same running total with no explicit contract about its state, so the coupon branch guessed wrong about whether the discount had already been applied. A seam replaces that guesswork with an explicit, identical contract every rule follows.
items.reference:
📈 Fighting: cost grows faster each round (interacts with every prior rule)
📉 Absorbing: one-time seam cost, then roughly flat per round
items.learnMore: In the unit's own numbers (2 hrs/round interaction penalty, seam introduced at round 2): fighting costs 2, 6, 12, 20 hours cumulative through rounds 1–4, while absorbing costs 2, 7, 9, 11 — identical at round 1, briefly costlier for absorbing at round 2 (the one-time seam setup), then cheaper and increasingly so from round 3 onward. Play with the interactive demo on this unit's L2 page to see the crossover move as you change the interaction penalty and which round the seam is introduced.

items.prompt: What does open-closed cost, concretely, in the pricing engine's round-2 fix?
choices: One extra concept (the PricingRule interface), an extra list to read, and one more level of indirection between reading the code and seeing what it does
Nothing — open-closed is always free once you learn it
It requires deleting all existing tests and rewriting them
It requires switching to a different programming language
items.explanation: Open-closed is a genuine trade, not a free win: the seam adds a concept to learn, a list to scan to know "what applies here," and an indirection layer — paid in exchange for existing rules staying untouched and independently testable.
items.reference:
💰 Bought: new rules can't reintroduce a bug in existing, tested rules
💸 Paid: one extra concept, one list to read, one indirection layer
items.learnMore: Open-closed is worth its price exactly when the alternative — editing a function with several rules already jammed into it — is more expensive than reading one extra interface. That crossover point is the actual judgment call: it isn't "always use open-closed" or "never use it," it's recognizing when the ledger tips in the seam's favor, which in Fernbridge's case was precisely when the second rule collided with the first.

items.prompt: What does open-closed buy, concretely, once the PricingRule seam exists?
choices: New rules can't reintroduce a round-2-style ordering bug in existing rules, since those are already tested and untouched by the new addition
The system becomes immune to all future bugs of any kind
The tax rate automatically adjusts itself with no code changes ever
It guarantees the code will never need another seam again
items.explanation: Because calculateTotal no longer contains rule-specific logic, adding a new rule can't touch — and therefore can't accidentally break — any existing rule's behavior or its tests. That's the specific thing bought, not a general immunity to bugs.
items.reference:

Never — it's purely theoretical and doesn't apply to real code

items.explanation: Open-closed is a trade evaluated case by case: it's worth its cost when modifying existing code to add a case would cost more than the seam's indirection — which is a judgment call tied to real signal, not a rule to apply to every function on principle.

Multi-currency was confirmed because Fernbridge is a global company

items.explanation: "More discount/fee rules" had one instance already in production, making a second plausible even before it arrived. "Multi-currency" had no signal at all — no customer request, no pending sales conversation — making it pure speculation rather than an unconfirmed-but-plausible axis.
items.reference:
✅ Confirmed signal — a second real variant has arrived

items.prompt: Why does this unit warn against building a seam for a purely speculative axis, even if the guess later turns out to be correct?
choices: Because the same reasoning, applied consistently, would also pay for the axes that never materialize — the cost is predictable only when it's tied to real evidence, not to guesses that sometimes happen to land
Because speculative axes are always wrong and never materialize
Because seams can only be built once per codebase, ever
Because YAGNI legally forbids writing interfaces
items.explanation: Even a guess that later turns out correct doesn't justify the reasoning that produced it — the same instinct applied to every hypothetical axis would pay the seam's cost repeatedly for axes that never show up. Tying seam introduction to real signal is what makes the cost predictable instead of a bet.

items.prompt: Round 3 brings both a VIP loyalty discount and a region-based tax rate change. Why do these need two separate seams instead of one shared seam?
choices: They're different axes of change — one adjusts the running total before tax, the other changes how tax itself is computed — so reusing one seam for both would force a mismatch
Because Fernbridge's coding standards require exactly two seams per feature
Because TypeScript doesn't allow two features to share an interface
There's no real reason — either seam would have worked equally well for both
items.explanation: The VIP discount is another instance of the same kind of thing PricingRule already models (a pre-tax adjustment). The regional tax rate is a structurally different axis — it changes tax computation itself, not the running total before tax — so it needs its own seam rather than a forced reuse of PricingRule.
items.reference:
🧩 Same axis → append to the existing seam
🆕 Different axis → build a new, purpose-built seam
items.learnMore: Forcing the tax-rate change through PricingRule — say, as a fake "rule" that multiplies by a tax-like negative amount — would recreate the same kind of implicit, undocumented coupling that caused the round-2 bug in the first place. A seam's shape is specific to the axis it protects; reusing it for a mismatched axis isn't reuse, it's a forced fit that tends to produce the same category of bug the original seam was built to prevent.

items.prompt: What would be wrong with reusing the existing PricingRule seam to implement the region-based tax rate, purely to avoid building a second seam?
choices: It would force a mismatch — PricingRule adjusts the pre-tax running total, while tax rate changes how tax is computed, so faking it as a rule reintroduces implicit, undocumented coupling
Nothing is wrong with it — one seam should always be reused for every future requirement
TypeScript would refuse to compile any second interface in the same file
It would make the code run measurably slower at runtime
items.explanation: Reusing a seam built for one axis to cover a structurally different axis recreates the same implicit-coupling problem the seam was meant to prevent — the fix isn't fewer seams, it's the right seam for each real axis of change.
items.reference:
🧩 Same axis → append to the existing seam
🆕 Different axis → build a new, purpose-built seam

items.prompt: What's the risk of building a seam for the wrong axis of change — e.g. a MultiCurrencyStrategy at round 0, before any customer requirement for it exists?
choices: Permanent indirection cost is paid every day, with no round of the system's life ever redeeming it, since the axis never actually varies
The code will fail to compile until the axis is actually used
There is no risk — extra seams never cost anything
It guarantees the design will need a rewrite within a year
items.explanation: A seam built for an axis that never gets a second real variant is pure overhead — the extra interface, list, or indirection layer costs something to read and maintain on every future change, with no round ever paying that cost back.
items.reference:
⏳ Too early: cost paid daily, redeemed never
🐌 Too late: each new if-branch fights every prior one
items.learnMore: The two failure directions are symmetric. Build the seam before there's a second variant, and you pay indirection forever for nothing — a PricingRule-equivalent list that stays at one entry for years is a seam nobody needed yet. Wait too long past the second variant, and every additional special case gets more expensive and more dangerous to add, because it has to be reasoned about against every prior special case sharing the same code path — the round-2 bug is exactly that failure mode.

items.prompt: What's the risk of the opposite mistake — waiting too long past the point where a second real variant already arrived and caused a problem?
choices: Each additional special case gets more expensive and more dangerous to add, since it must be reasoned about against every prior special case sharing the same code path
There is no risk to waiting — later is always strictly better than earlier
The code becomes literally impossible to change at all
It only affects performance, never correctness
items.explanation: Stacking a third, fourth, fifth if onto a function that already produced a bug at the second one compounds the risk — each new branch interacts with every prior one, which is precisely the mechanism behind the round-2 coupon/discount bug, and it gets worse with every additional branch left unaddressed.

📈 Fighting: cost per round grows with prior rules
➖ Absorbing: flat per round after the one-time seam cost
items.learnMore: In the unit's numbers (2 hrs/round interaction penalty, seam introduced at round 2): fighting's cumulative cost is 2, 6, 12, 20 hours through rounds 1–4; absorbing's is 2, 7, 9, 11. Both start identical at round 1, absorbing briefly costs more at round 2 (the seam's one-time price), then the gap opens and keeps opening every round after — try the interactive demo on this unit's L2 page and drag the interaction-penalty slider to see how much the widening gap depends on how tangled the fighting version's rules actually are.

items.prompt: Implement a PricingRule named "volume-discount" that applies a 10% discount to the running total whenever it exceeds $500, and leaves it unchanged otherwise. The rule receives `(total: number)` and returns the adjusted total.

tests.description: no discount at or under the threshold
10% off above the threshold
unaffected total stays exact for small orders

items.explanation: The rule only needs the running total to decide — that's the entire contract every PricingRule follows. Applying the 10% discount only when total exceeds the threshold, and returning the unmodified total otherwise, matches Fernbridge's round-1 requirement exactly, now expressed as an appendable object instead of an inline if-statement.
items.reference:
Question: implement a PricingRule for a discount tied to the running total.
📐 Contract: apply(total) (or apply(total, order)) → new total
💵 Discount depends only on the running total / order fields, never on subtotal directly
items.learnMore: Every PricingRule in Fernbridge's engine shares one contract: take the running total (and the order, for rules that need more context), return the new running total. That uniform contract is what makes rules composable in an array via reduce — no rule needs to know how many other rules exist or what order they ran in, only what the running total looks like when it's called. See this unit's L3 for the full round-1-to-round-3 walkthrough this rule comes from.

items.prompt: Implement a PricingRule named "loyalty-tier" that applies a 5% discount to the running total when the order's `customerTier` is `"vip"`, and leaves it unchanged for any other tier (including `undefined`). The rule receives `(total, order)`.

tests.description: 5% off for a vip customer
unaffected for a standard customer
unaffected when customerTier is missing

items.explanation: This rule needs the order object, not just the running total, to know the customer's tier — the PricingRule contract's second parameter exists exactly for cases like this. Guarding with a strict equality check against "vip" handles missing/undefined tiers correctly by falling through to the unchanged branch.

items.prompt: Implement a PricingRule named "bulk-tier" that applies a 15% discount to the running total whenever it exceeds $1000, and a 10% discount when it's between $500 and $1000 inclusive, and leaves it unchanged below $500. The rule receives `(total)`.

tests.description: no discount below 500
10% off at exactly 500
15% off above 1000

items.explanation: A single rule can encapsulate several thresholds of the same kind of adjustment (all pre-tax percentage discounts) without needing to be split into multiple PricingRule objects — the seam's granularity is 'one behaviorally distinct adjustment,' not 'one if-branch.'

items.prompt: Implement a PricingRule named "coupon" that subtracts `order.couponAmount` from the running total (if present), never letting the result go below 0. The rule receives `(total, order)`.

tests.description: subtracts the coupon amount when present
leaves total unchanged with no coupon
floors at 0 instead of going negative

items.explanation: This is the rule that, when written directly against subtotal instead of the running total in Fernbridge's original buggy version, silently canceled the volume discount. Written correctly against the PricingRule contract's `total` parameter, it always operates on whatever the running total is after every prior rule — no guessing about pre- or post-discount state required.
items.reference:
Question: implement the coupon rule that caused Fernbridge's round-2 bug when done wrong.
🐛 Bug: written against subtotal instead of total
✅ Fix: always operate on the running total argument
items.learnMore: Fernbridge's actual round-2 bug came from a coupon branch that recomputed subtotal - order.couponAmount instead of using the running total already adjusted by the volume discount — silently erasing that discount whenever a coupon was present. The PricingRule contract removes the ambiguity: total is always whatever the prior rules left it as, so there's no separate 'original subtotal' to accidentally fall back to.

items.prompt: Implement a PricingRule named "percentage-coupon" that subtracts a percentage-based coupon (`order.couponPercent`, e.g. 0.15 for 15% off) from the running total, if present, never letting the result go below 0. The rule receives `(total, order)`.

tests.description: applies a 15% coupon to the running total
leaves total unchanged with no coupon
never goes negative even with a coupon over 100%

items.explanation: A percentage-based coupon is still the same kind of adjustment as the flat-dollar coupon rule — both operate on whatever the running total is when they're called, which is exactly why they can coexist in the same PricingRule list without conflicting.

items.prompt: Given an existing `runPricingRules(subtotal, order, rules)` function (below) and an existing `defaultRules` array with a `volumeDiscountRule` already in it, append a new `vipLoyaltyRule` (5% off for `order.customerTier === "vip"`) to a *new* array WITHOUT mutating `defaultRules`, then run it. This tests that extension doesn't require editing the existing array or function.

tests.description: applies both volume discount and vip loyalty for a vip order over 500
defaultRules is not mutated by the extension
standard-tier order only gets the volume discount

items.explanation: Using the spread operator to build a new array (`[...defaultRules, vipLoyaltyRule]`) instead of `defaultRules.push(...)` is what keeps this genuinely an extension rather than a modification — the original array, and anything else in the codebase still referencing it, is left completely untouched. This is the exact mechanism that let round 3's VIP rule ship without re-testing volumeDiscountRule.
items.reference:
Question: add a new rule without mutating the existing rules array.
➕ Extension: [...defaultRules, newRule]
🚫 Not: defaultRules.push(newRule)
items.learnMore: Open-closed isn't just about not editing function bodies — it also means not mutating shared data structures that other code might still reference in their original form. Building a new array via spread, rather than mutating defaultRules in place, is what let Fernbridge's round-3 VIP rule ship as a pure addition: every existing test written against defaultRules for volumeDiscountRule and couponRule kept passing unmodified.

items.prompt: Given the same setup, append a new `processingFeeWaiverRule` that adds a flat $15 to the running total unless `order.hasProcessingFee` is falsy or the running total exceeds 1000 (i.e. add $15 only when `hasProcessingFee` is true AND the running total is <= 1000). Extend without mutating `defaultRules`.

tests.description: adds the $15 fee when eligible and under threshold
no fee added when hasProcessingFee is false
defaultRules stays untouched

items.explanation: The fee check is deliberately written against the running total (post-discount), so its threshold decision is a visible, explicit choice — not an implicit guess about whether it should see the pre- or post-discount amount, which is exactly the ambiguity that caused round 2's real bug.

items.prompt: Given the same setup, write `withTwoNewRules(order)` that appends BOTH a `roundingRule` (rounds the running total to the nearest whole dollar using `Math.round`) and a `minimumChargeRule` (bumps the running total up to a $5 minimum if it's below $5) — in that order — without mutating `defaultRules`.

tests.description: rounds and applies the minimum charge for a tiny order
rounds a mid-size order with no minimum-charge kick-in
defaultRules is still untouched after two appends

items.explanation: Order matters here — rounding before applying the minimum charge means a rounded 2.4 -> 2 would still trigger the minimum, while the reverse order could produce a different result. Because the seam makes the array order visible and explicit, that ordering decision is a one-line fact to read, not a hidden assumption buried in nested if-statements.

items.prompt: The buggy `calculateTotal` below recomputes the coupon discount against `subtotal` instead of the already-discounted `running` value, silently erasing the volume discount whenever a coupon is present. Fix ONLY the coupon line so both discounts stack correctly (function signature and rounding must stay the same).

tests.description: stacks volume discount and coupon correctly
still correct with no coupon at all
still correct for a small order with a coupon and no volume discount

items.explanation: Reading `running - order.couponAmount` instead of `subtotal - order.couponAmount` stacks the coupon on top of whatever adjustments already happened, instead of overwriting them. This one-line fix removes the immediate symptom, but the real fix this unit argues for is the structural one in the next pool — a PricingRule seam that makes this kind of overwrite impossible by contract, not just fixed by a careful reread.
items.reference:
Question: find and fix the exact line that caused Fernbridge's round-2 bug.
🐛 Bug: running = subtotal - coupon
✅ Fix: running = running - coupon
items.learnMore: This patch is a real, valid fix — but notice it only fixes this specific pair of rules. A third rule added the same sloppy way (reading from subtotal instead of the current running value) would reintroduce the exact same class of bug. That's why L3's actual fix isn't a corrected if-statement, it's replacing the shared-mutable-variable pattern entirely with a PricingRule contract where every rule's only input is the current running total — making the overwrite mistake structurally impossible, not just fixed this once.

items.prompt: A similar bug: the processing-fee waiver below checks `subtotal <= 1000` instead of checking against the discounted running total, so a $1200 order that drops to $980 after a big coupon still wrongly gets denied the fee waiver. Fix ONLY the fee condition so it checks the running total, not the original subtotal.

tests.description: fee waiver now correctly triggers based on the discounted total
tests.expr: expect(calculateTotal({ items: [{ description: "x", amount: 1200 }], couponAmount: 220, hasProcessingFee: true })).toBe(1073.4)

tests.description: fee still charged for an order that stays above 1000 after coupon
tests.expr: expect(calculateTotal({ items: [{ description: "x", amount: 1200 }], couponAmount: 100, hasProcessingFee: true })).toBe(1188)

tests.description: no fee logic engaged when hasProcessingFee is false
tests.expr: expect(calculateTotal({ items: [{ description: "x", amount: 1200 }], couponAmount: 220, hasProcessingFee: false })).toBe(1058.4)

items.explanation: Checking `running` instead of `subtotal` makes the fee decision consistent with whatever the coupon already did — the same class of bug as the volume-discount/coupon collision, just on a different pair of rules, which is exactly why this unit argues the fix belongs at the structural level (a shared contract), not in each individual condition.

items.prompt: Implement `calculateTotal(order, rules)` using a PricingRule seam: sum `order.items[].amount` for the subtotal, reduce it through `rules` (each rule receives `(total, order)`), then apply an 8% tax to the result and round to 2 decimals.

tests.description: no rules: just subtotal plus tax
one rule applied before tax
tests.expr: expect(calculateTotal({ items: [{ amount: 600 }] }, [{ apply: (t) => t - t * 0.1 }])).toBe(583.2)

tests.description: two rules applied in array order before tax
tests.expr: expect(calculateTotal({ items: [{ amount: 600 }] }, [{ apply: (t) => t - t * 0.1 }, { apply: (t) => t - 20 }])).toBe(561.6)

items.explanation: This is Fernbridge's actual round-2-fixed calculateTotal: it contains no rule-specific logic at all, only the generic pipeline (sum items, reduce through whatever rules were passed, tax, round). That's what makes it closed for modification — a new rule never requires touching this function's body again.
items.reference:
Question: implement the generic pipeline function every rule plugs into.
➡️ subtotal → reduce(rules) → tax → round
items.learnMore: The array order passed into rules is now the single, visible place the business's adjustment order lives — previously that order was implicit in which if-statement happened to be written first or last, and easy to get wrong (as round 2 proved). Reading the array top to bottom tells you the exact order adjustments apply in, without needing to trace through nested conditionals.

items.prompt: Implement `calculateTotal(order, rules, resolveTaxRate)` — same pipeline as before, but the tax rate now comes from calling `resolveTaxRate(order)` instead of a hardcoded 8%, so a region-specific tax resolver can be swapped in without touching this function.

tests.description: flat 8% resolver behaves like before
a region-aware resolver changes the tax rate without touching this function
rules still apply before tax regardless of resolver
tests.expr: expect(calculateTotal({ items: [{ amount: 600 }] }, [{ apply: (t) => t - t * 0.1 }], () => 0.08)).toBe(583.2)

items.explanation: This is round 3's second seam — a TaxRateResolver function parameter — introduced only once a real region-based tax requirement arrived, deliberately separate from the PricingRule seam because it protects a different axis (how tax is computed, not what the pre-tax total is).

items.prompt: Implement a `regionAwareTaxRate(order)` TaxRateResolver function: return 0.20 for `order.region === "EU"`, 0.05 for `order.region === "CA"`, and 0.08 for anything else (including missing region).

tests.description: EU rate
CA rate
default rate for no region

items.explanation: This resolver is a self-contained function with no dependency on PricingRule at all — it's a deliberately separate seam for a separate axis (how tax is computed), added only once a real multi-region tax requirement showed up, not guessed at back when the pricing engine had only one discount rule.
items.reference:
Question: implement a TaxRateResolver — a seam for a different axis than PricingRule.
🌍 Tax rate varies by region, not by pre-tax rule
items.learnMore: Forcing this into a fake PricingRule (e.g. a rule that subtracts a tax-shaped amount from the running total) would blur the pre-tax adjustment total with the post-tax bill, recreating exactly the kind of implicit coupling that caused the round-2 bug. Keeping it a separate, small function parameter is what lets each seam stay simple and its own axis stay legible.

items.prompt: Implement a `tieredTaxRate(order)` TaxRateResolver: return 0.0 (tax-exempt) when `order.taxExempt` is true, otherwise fall back to `order.region === "EU" ? 0.20 : 0.08`. Tax-exempt status must always win regardless of region.

tests.description: tax-exempt overrides region entirely
EU rate when not exempt
default rate when neither exempt nor EU

items.explanation: Checking taxExempt first, before the region logic, makes the precedence explicit and readable in one glance — the same principle the PricingRule array order made visible for pre-tax adjustments now applies inside this resolver's own internal ordering.
